content: 1. Rifampin reduces the effectiveness of etonogestrel by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 enzymes, leading to increased metabolism of the drug. It is recommended to avoid rifampin or use an alternative medication. Close monitoring is advised if co-administration is necessary. 2. Rifapentine also decreases the levels and efficacy of etonogestrel through CYP3A4 enzyme induction. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is required when these drugs are used together. 3. Ritonavir increases the levels and effects of etonogestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely when these drugs are co-administered. 4. Rufinamide decreases the levels and effectiveness of etonogestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 5. St. John’s Wort significantly reduces the levels and efficacy of etonogestrel by inducing CYP3A4 enzymes. It is strongly recommended to avoid St. John’s Wort or use an alternative medication. 6. Sugammadex reduces the effectiveness of etonogestrel by competing for receptor binding. In vitro studies suggest that sugammadex binds to progestogens, decreasing their exposure. A bolus dose of sugammadex is considered equivalent to missing doses of hormonal contraceptives. If sugammadex is administered, patients using oral, transdermal, or implantable hormonal contraceptives must use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method (e.g., condoms, spermicides) for the next 7 days. 7. Topiramate decreases the levels and efficacy of etonogestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. 8. Verapamil increases the levels and effects of etonogestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely when these drugs are co-administered. 9. Voriconazole increases the levels and effects of etonogestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 10. Zafirlukast increases the levels and effects of etonogestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely when these drugs are co-administered. 11. Common side effects of etonogestrel implants include back pain, depression, dizziness, dysmenorrhea, emotional lability, flu-like symptoms, insertion-site pain, nausea, nervousness, and general pain. Gastrointestinal disorders such as constipation, diarrhea, flatulence, and vomiting may occur. General conditions like edema, fatigue, implant site reactions, and fever have been reported. Immune system reactions, including anaphylaxis, are rare. Infections such as rhinitis and urinary tract infections may occur. Investigations have shown clinically relevant increases in blood pressure and weight loss in some cases. 12. Musculoskeletal complaints include arthralgia, musculoskeletal pain, and myalgia. Nervous system disorders such as convulsions, migraines, and somnolence have been reported. Reproductive system issues include breast discharge, breast enlargement, ovarian cysts, genital pruritus, and vulvovaginal discomfort. Skin disorders include angioedema, alopecia, chloasma, hypertrichosis, pruritus, rash, seborrhea, and urticaria. Vascular disorders such as hot flushes and chest pain, as well as respiratory issues like dyspnea, cough, or hemoptysis, have been documented when implants migrate to the pulmonary artery. 13. Etonogestrel implants are contraindicated in individuals with known or suspected breast cancer, a history of progestin-sensitive cancers, active liver disease, or liver tumors. They should not be used in cases of undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding or hypersensitivity to etonogestrel or its components. Patients with a history of thromboembolic disorders, thrombophlebitis, or conditions exacerbated by fluid retention (e.g., migraines, asthma, epilepsy) should use this medication with caution. 14. Women with a family history of breast cancer or those who develop breast nodules should be closely monitored. Due to the risk of thromboembolism associated with pregnancy and the postpartum period, etonogestrel should not be used within 21 days postpartum. Discontinue use if jaundice, severe depression, visual disturbances, or signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE) develop. 15. Contact lens wearers experiencing visual changes or lens intolerance should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist. Retinal vein thrombosis should be ruled out in cases of unexplained vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, or retinal vascular lesions. Discontinue the implant 4 weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 16. Women with hypertension or renal disease should avoid hormonal contraception unless their condition is well-controlled. If sustained hypertension develops during therapy, the implant should be removed. Annual blood pressure checks are recommended for all patients using etonogestrel implants. 17. Broken or bent implants may increase the release rate of etonogestrel. Ensure complete removal of the implant during extraction. Hormonal contraceptives may slightly increase the risk of gallbladder disease, though this is not well-documented for progestin-only methods. 18. Monitor prediabetic and diabetic women receiving etonogestrel therapy, as it may induce mild insulin resistance and alter glucose concentrations. Women with hyperlipidemia should also be monitored closely, as some progestins may elevate LDL levels and complicate lipid control. 19. Enlarged ovarian follicles may occur due to delayed atresia, but they typically resolve spontaneously. Rarely, surgical intervention may be required. Sex hormone-binding globulin concentrations may decrease for the first six months after implant insertion, followed by gradual recovery. 20. Restart contraception immediately after implant removal if continued contraceptive protection is desired. Etonogestrel is contraindicated during pregnancy, as there is no need for contraception in pregnant women. Epidemiologic studies have not shown an increased risk of birth defects with prior exposure to low-dose combined hormonal contraceptives. 21. Small amounts of etonogestrel may be present in breast milk, but no significant adverse effects on milk production, quality, or infant development have been observed. However, hormonal contraceptives may reduce milk production in some breastfeeding mothers, particularly if breastfeeding is not well-established. Non-hormonal contraceptive options should be considered for nursing mothers. 22. Etonogestrel inhibits gonadotropin secretion, preventing follicular maturation and ovulation. It also increases cervical mucus viscosity and stimulates mammary tissue growth. The drug is highly bioavailable (100%), with 98% protein binding (32% to SHBG, 66% to albumin). It is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4 enzymes, has a half-life of 25 hours, and is excreted primarily in urine and feces.
